text: Could you pick one recent customer complaint where the investigation changed an important decision?
A customer found a brake-housing serial number that did not match the lot in our certificate. They gave us forty-eight hours for containment and a formal response.
What did you look at first?
The complaint was in QMS and SAP had the formal lot history, but a quality spreadsheet tracked serial-number exceptions. An email from second shift connected the exception to a relabeling window.
What explanation did the team start with?
We first blamed an operator scan mistake because that had happened once before. The spreadsheet made it look plausible, but it did not explain why three serials shared the same gap.
What separated that theory from the alternatives?
Maintenance logs showed the scanner rebooted during the exact relabeling window. That shifted us from individual operator error to a system synchronization failure.
We widened containment from two lots to nine because the serial-number mismatch crossed the assumed shift boundary. I recommended the change during the response call.
I do not remember. The approval happened on the call, and the meeting note only records the decision, not the person's name.
IT added a reconciliation check between the scanner queue and SAP. Quality also stopped maintaining the serial exception spreadsheet after the open entries were migrated.
How did the customer judge whether it worked?
They accepted three clean shipments plus our reconciliation report. We had no repeat mismatch in the next six weeks.
Where did the official process differ from the work you actually did?

The procedure says QMS owns the evidence trail, but the decisive links came from SAP, the spreadsheet, maintenance logs, and email. My next action is to ask the response-call owner to add named decision owners to the meeting record.
